\title{Distribution-Preserving QIM: Histogram Detectability
and Robustness Trade-offs in Invisible Watermarking}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Abhishek Sairam Gaduputi}
\IEEEauthorblockA{Department of Data Science\\
New Jersey Institute of Technology\\
Newark, NJ 07102, USA\\
ag2936@njit.edu}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Quantization index modulation (QIM) leaves a lattice fingerprint in DCT
coefficients. We study Distribution-Preserving QIM (DP-QIM), which replaces
a mismatched carrier with a sample from a target quantile cell rather than
a lattice point. We derive an idealized cellwise mixture formula and a
positive-scaling property restricted to a zero decision boundary; neither
guarantees exact distribution preservation or image-level robustness.
Corrected experiments use 43 crops from 14 deduplicated photographs, one
outer source split for all detector fitting and calibration, and conditional
source-bootstrap intervals. At 64 bits, learned-histogram detector AUC is
$0.65\,[0.63,0.76]$ for DP-QIM versus $0.95\,[0.91,1.00]$ for QIM; DP-QIM's
AUC rises to $0.84$ at 256 bits and $0.96$ at 1,024 bits. DP-QIM is therefore
detectable, not statistically invisible. At the same DCT position and
interpolated matched PSNR, it gains approximately $35$, $33$, and $21$
percentage points in bit accuracy under blur, half-resolution downscaling,
and half-contrast processing, respectively. It loses approximately $16$ and
$29$ points under JPEG qualities 90 and 70, $14$ under additive noise, and
$3$ to $7$ under a simplified histogram-jitter attack. These small-sample
results characterize a robustness/detectability trade-off, not security
against strong steganalysis or the original UnMarker attack. Code and
correction records are released.\footnote{\url{https://github.com/sairam782/Invisible-Watermarking}}
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
invisible watermarking, quantization index modulation, DCT, steganalysis,
valumetric scaling, AI-generated content provenance
\end{IEEEkeywords}

%------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Invisible watermarks are a primary tool for tracing the provenance of images,
including AI-generated ones~\cite{Cox2007book}. Recent work shows they are
fragile against adaptive adversaries. UnMarker~\cite{Kassis2025unmarker}
removes deployed watermarks without access to the detector or the key by
locating spectral regions whose statistics differ from those of natural images
and perturbing them, and regeneration attacks remove watermarks by re-synthesizing
the image~\cite{Zhao2023removable,Erasing2024neurips}.

Quantization index modulation (QIM)~\cite{Chen2001qim} and its descendants are
especially exposed to the first kind of attack. QIM writes each carrier
coefficient onto one of two interleaved lattices, so the marginal histogram of
watermarked coefficients collapses onto isolated spikes
(Fig.~\ref{fig:hist}, middle), a fingerprint natural images do not have.
This paper asks a narrow question: \emph{if a QIM-style watermark is
constrained to leave the coefficient marginal natural, what does it gain and
what does it lose?}

We study Distribution-Preserving QIM (DP-QIM). It partitions the empirical
distribution of a coefficient into $2M$ equal-mass cells with alternating bit
labels; a coefficient already in a cell carrying its bit is left unchanged,
and otherwise it is replaced by a natural sample drawn from the interior of an
adjacent cell. Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The DP-QIM embedding rule and two scoped properties: an idealized
cellwise mixture formula (Prop.~\ref{prop:ks}), and positive-scaling invariance
at a zero boundary contrasted with periodic QIM decoding (Prop.~\ref{prop:scale}).
\item A content-audited comparison protocol for quantization watermarks: both
methods at the same DCT position, robustness curves compared at matched PSNR,
cross-validation grouped by deduplicated source photograph, training-only
detector fitting and calibration, and conditional bootstrap confidence intervals
(Sec.~\ref{sec:protocol}).
\item An empirical characterization of the trade-off on real photographs:
histogram detectability and gains under some scaling-type attacks, paid for
with reduced margin against requantization and additive noise
(Sec.~\ref{sec:results}).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\textwidth]{figures/fig1_histograms_v2.pdf}

%------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\textbf{QIM and its variants.} QIM~\cite{Chen2001qim} and dither modulation
are provably good under additive noise~\cite{PerezGonzalez2003knownhost} but
fragile to valumetric (amplitude) scaling. Rational dither
modulation~\cite{PerezGonzalez2005rdm}, angle QIM~\cite{Ourique2005angleqim}
and perceptually scaled QIM~\cite{Li2007perceptualqim} restore scaling
robustness by making the quantizer gain-adaptive. These schemes still write onto
a (scaled) lattice; one-cell-boundary DP-QIM is scale-invariant only when that
boundary is zero. Our focus is the joint empirical behaviour of histogram
detectability and robustness, not a claim of new scaling invariance. We
do not compare against these gain-invariant variants
(Sec.~\ref{sec:limitations}).

\textbf{Learned watermarks.} HiDDeN~\cite{Zhu2018hidden},
StegaStamp~\cite{Tancik2020stegastamp}, Stable
Signature~\cite{Fernandez2023stablesignature} and
InvisMark~\cite{Xu2025invismark} train encoder-decoder networks against
differentiable distortion layers. They are robust to common processing but
remain vulnerable to regeneration~\cite{Zhao2023removable} and to
UnMarker~\cite{Kassis2025unmarker}. Analogous statistical-signature concerns
arise for language-model watermarks~\cite{Kirchenbauer2023llmwatermark}.

\textbf{Steganalysis and distribution preservation.} Steganography seeks to
hide the \emph{existence} of a message from statistical
detectors~\cite{Fridrich2009stegobook,Fridrich2012richmodels}, and
distribution-preserving embedding is a classical tool there. We borrow that
goal for robust watermarking, where the adversary's aim is removal rather than
detection, and measure undetectability with steganalysis-style detectors.

%------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Distribution-Preserving QIM}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{Setting}
An RGB image is converted to YCbCr (BT.601) and the luminance is split into
$8{\times}8$ blocks with orthonormal 2-D DCT. A payload of $P$ bits is carried
by one coefficient position $(u,v)$ in $P$ blocks chosen by a keyed
permutation over interior blocks (blocks touching reflect-padding are excluded
because padding is re-derived from modified pixels at decode time). Both
methods below use the same position and block selection on our block-aligned crops.

\textbf{DCT-QIM baseline.} Dither-modulation QIM~\cite{Chen2001qim} with step
$\Delta$ snaps the carrier $c$ to $L_b = \{k\Delta + b\Delta/2\}$ and decodes
by the nearer of $L_0, L_1$.

\subsection{Embedding rule}
Let $F$ be the empirical CDF of coefficient $(u,v)$ over a training set of
natural images. For $M\geq1$, quantile boundaries
$F^{-1}(i/2M)$, $i=0,\dots,2M$, define cells $\mathcal{C}_0,\dots,\mathcal{C}_{2M-1}$
of approximately equal empirical mass with labels $\ell_i = i \bmod 2$;
ties can prevent exact equality. For a safety margin
$\epsilon>0$, the \emph{safe pool} $\mathcal{P}_i$ holds training coefficients
that lie in $\mathcal{C}_i$ at least $\epsilon$ from its finite boundaries.
To embed bit $b$ in a carrier $c$ with cell index $k$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item if $\ell_k = b$, leave $c$ unchanged;
\item otherwise, draw one keyed sample from each adjacent pool
$\mathcal{P}_{k\pm1}$ and replace $c$ with the one closer to $c$.
\end{enumerate}
The decoder returns the label of the cell containing the received
coefficient. All experiments use $M=1$; larger $M$ produced narrow cells near
the mode that did not survive 8-bit rounding.

\subsection{Properties}

\begin{proposition}[marginal]
\label{prop:ks}
Let $M=1$ and let a continuous carrier distribution $F$ be split at its median
into cells $C_0,C_1$, each of probability $1/2$. Assume independent uniform
payload bits and ideal independent sampling. Let $G_{i,\epsilon}$ be $F$
conditioned on cell $C_i$ and distance at least $\epsilon$ from the boundary,
with positive safe mass in each cell. Then
\[
 P_W=\tfrac12F+\tfrac14G_{0,\epsilon}+\tfrac14G_{1,\epsilon}.
\]
Writing $G_\epsilon=(G_{0,\epsilon}+G_{1,\epsilon})/2$ gives
$\mathrm{KS}(P_W,F)=\tfrac12\mathrm{KS}(G_\epsilon,F)\to0$ as
$\epsilon\to0$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}[Sketch]
Each carrier is unchanged with probability $1/2$, independently of its value.
A mismatch from each original cell occurs with probability $1/4$ and draws
from the other cell's safe conditional law. This yields the mixture.
Continuity implies zero mass at the median, so the two safe conditional laws
converge to the original cellwise laws as the margin vanishes. Their equally
weighted mixture therefore converges to $F$; the KS identity follows by
subtracting the common component.
\end{proof}

Importantly, $G_\epsilon$ is not generally $F$ conditioned globally on being
outside the margin: the two cells can lose different amounts of mass.
For example, safe masses in ratio $3:1$ yield global conditional weights
$3/4:1/4$, not the sampler's $1/2:1/2$. This idealized result is not an exact
guarantee for our capped 512-sample pools, empirical ties, or RGB rounding.
For continuous $F$, a fixed lattice produces a different distribution, but
there is no uniform positive KS lower bound as the lattice spacing tends to zero.

\begin{proposition}[scaling]
\label{prop:scale}
Let an attack map the carrier $c \mapsto s\,c$ for some $s>0$.
(i) If the $M{=}1$ cell boundary is $0$, the DP-QIM decision $\mathbb{1}\{c\geq0\}$
is unchanged for every $s>0$.
(ii) For a QIM carrier $c\in L_b$, away from decision ties, decoding preserves
$b$ iff $d_\Delta((s-1)c)<\Delta/4$, where
$d_\Delta(x)=\min_{k\in\mathbb Z}|x-k\Delta|$.
Thus $|1-s||c|<\Delta/4$ is sufficient but not necessary.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}[Sketch]
(i) Positive scaling preserves the two half-lines and zero. (ii) Points in
the original label's lattice are separated by $\Delta$, and each has a
decision interval of radius $\Delta/4$. Decoding depends on displacement
modulo $\Delta$, not total displacement. At equal-distance ties the code
chooses bit 0. The strict bound around the original point is sufficient.
\end{proof}

For example, $\Delta=16$, $c=32$, and $s=1/2$ preserve bit 0 even though
the displacement is 16, disproving the earlier necessary-condition claim.
The sign result requires an exactly zero fitted boundary; the released audit
records each training-fold boundary. Blur and resizing are not generally
independent scalar maps on block-DCT coefficients. Even an ideal two-dimensional
Gaussian has attenuation $e^{-2\pi^2\sigma^2(f_x^2+f_y^2)}$, rather than a
one-axis expression. Boundary mixing, clipping, and integer rounding require
empirical evaluation; the proposition does not guarantee blur or resize robustness.

%------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Evaluation Protocol}
\label{sec:protocol}

\textbf{Data.} We use the real photographs distributed with scikit-image and
Matplotlib (outdoor and indoor scenes, a portrait, natural textures, and
astronomical and microscopy images; synthetic and text images excluded): 14
distinct sources, cut into 43 non-overlapping $256{\times}256$ crops (at most
four per source). We exclude the \texttt{cat} alias of \texttt{chelsea},
deduplicate full-image hashes, and reject duplicate crop hashes. Missing sources
raise errors rather than silently changing the dataset.

\textbf{Splits.} Five folds are grouped by \emph{source}, so no test crop
shares a photograph with any training crop. DP-QIM's CDF and pools, and the
attacker's natural reference, are fitted on training sources only. Every crop
is tested exactly once. Crop hashes, fold assignments, dependency versions,
and calibration parameters are saved with the corrected v3 results.

\textbf{Matched fidelity.} Both methods embed $P{=}64$ bits at the same
position (main results at $(3,3)$). We sweep DP-QIM's margin
$\epsilon\in\{0.5,1,2,3,4,6\}$ and QIM's step
$\Delta\in\{6,8,10,12,16,20,24,32,40,48,56,64,80,96,128\}$, and compare
DP-QIM against the QIM curve linearly interpolated to DP-QIM's mean PSNR. We
never extrapolate beyond the sweep. This is a descriptive comparison of held-out
fidelity-robustness curves, not training-time selection of a deployed parameter.
We retain $\epsilon=2$ from the previous pilot as the main operating point;
it is not selected anew to maximize the corrected results.

\textbf{Attacks.} JPEG ($Q{=}90,70$), additive Gaussian noise ($\sigma{=}0.03$
of full range), Pillow Gaussian blur (radius 1), $0.5\times$ bicubic
down-and-up-scaling, and contrast scaling about the image mean by $0.5$ and
$0.8$ (amplitude scaling before clipping and 8-bit rounding).

\textbf{Histogram-jitter removal.} Inspired by statistical-anomaly attacks,
we use a simplified stress test, not a reproduction of
UnMarker~\cite{Kassis2025unmarker}. For each of the 63 AC positions the
attacker compares the received image's coefficient histogram with a natural
reference built from \emph{training-source} images, flags bins whose density
exceeds the reference by a ratio $\tau$, and adds Gaussian jitter of $j$ times
the reference inter-quartile range to coefficients in flagged bins. The
attacker never sees the embedder's pools or key, but its reference and the
embedder's CDF use the same training photos and are not statistically
independent. We apply identical attack parameters to both methods; realized
distortion can differ, and per-image attacked PSNR is recorded.

\textbf{Detectors.} (a) A learned detector: logistic regression on the
1-unit-bin histogram of the carrier position over \emph{all} blocks of an
image. Following Kerckhoffs' principle it knows the method and position, but
not the block-selection seed. (b) An unsupervised histogram peak
statistic: the maximum over-density of the image's histogram relative to a
reference built from the outer training sources. At each of five outer
source folds and each $P\in\{64,256,1024\}$, we fit the DP-QIM CDF on training
crops, construct training watermarks, and choose QIM's $\Delta$ from
$\{4,6,\ldots,64\}$ by nearest training-mean PSNR to DP-QIM. The histogram
scaler and logistic model ($C=0.1$) are fitted on training cover/stego pairs
only. We then encode and score the held-out crops without refitting or
test-based calibration. Held-out PSNR can differ between methods and is reported.

\textbf{Statistics.} Detector ROC-AUC is calculated within each fold and
averaged with held-out crop-count weights; raw scores from different fitted
models are never ranked against one another. All table 95\% confidence
intervals use 2{,}000 whole-source bootstrap resamples. These intervals are
conditional on the fixed fitted models and split, not uncertainty over
retraining, new splits, or populations. Payload bits are seeded by CRC32
of the crop name. One fixed block-selection seed is a further limitation.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Detectability}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Crop-weighted within-fold detector ROC-AUC with conditional 95\%
source-bootstrap CI (0.5 = chance). Position $(3,3)$, DP-QIM $\epsilon=2$;
QIM fidelity calibrated on training data. PSNR column reports DP-QIM.}
\label{tab:detect}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/detect.tex}}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:detect} shows substantial DP-QIM detectability: learned AUC
increases from 0.65 to 0.84 and 0.96 as payload increases from 64 to 256 and
1,024 bits. QIM gives 0.95, 1.00 and 1.00. Thus the corrected evaluation does
not support our earlier near-undetectability claim. Held-out mean PSNR is
53.36 versus 53.66~dB at 64 bits, 46.94 versus 47.12~dB at 256 bits, and
40.96 versus 41.07~dB at 1,024 bits (DP-QIM versus QIM). These residual
gaps follow from training-only calibration and should not be hidden.

The fixed-direction peak score is weaker against DP-QIM (0.47, 0.50,
0.62). An AUC below 0.5 is not evidence of security: score inversion can
recover discriminatory information, and the learned detector already
distinguishes the classes. Finite sampling, margin exclusions, and image
conversion can leave detectable structure even when the histogram looks similar.
We do not isolate the relative contributions of those mechanisms here.

\subsection{Robustness at matched fidelity}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Bit accuracy of DP-QIM ($\epsilon=2$, 53.4~dB, position $(3,3)$,
64 bits) and difference from PSNR-interpolated QIM. Bold: conditional
95\% source-bootstrap CI excludes zero.}
\label{tab:robust}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/robustness.tex}}
\end{table}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\textwidth]{figures/fig2_curves_v2.pdf}
\caption{Bit accuracy versus watermarked-image PSNR on 43 crops, position
$(3,3)$, 64 bits. QIM is a step-size sweep; DP-QIM points vary the safety margin.
These empirical processing trade-offs are not general security guarantees.}
\label{fig:curves}
\end{figure*}

Table~\ref{tab:robust} and Fig.~\ref{fig:curves} retain an empirical split.
DP-QIM gains 34.8~pp under blur, 33.4~pp under downscaling, and 20.8~pp under
half contrast; corresponding accuracies are 0.841, 0.826 and 0.967.
These are measured image-level outcomes, not consequences guaranteed by
Prop.~\ref{prop:scale}. At contrast $\times0.8$, the difference is $-0.4$~pp
with an interval spanning zero. Under JPEG 90, JPEG 70 and additive noise,
DP-QIM loses 15.8, 28.6 and 14.1~pp. This is consistent with less perturbation
margin when sampling ordinary carrier values, but does not establish a
universal ordering outside the tested data and parameters.

\subsection{Removal stress test}
The simplified histogram-jitter attack gives DP-QIM bit accuracy 0.973
($\tau=2,j=0.5$) and 0.912 ($\tau=1.5,j=1$), respectively 2.7 and 7.0~pp
below matched QIM. This does not demonstrate resistance to published UnMarker
or adaptive removal. Reduced peak-score AUC does not prevent selective
attacks: the learned detector distinguishes DP-QIM images.

\subsection{Effect of position}
\label{sec:ablation}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Gain (pp) of DP-QIM ($\epsilon=2$) over PSNR-interpolated QIM at
three DCT positions. Bold: conditional 95\% source-bootstrap CI excludes zero.}
\label{tab:ablation}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/ablation.tex}}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:ablation} repeats the comparison at $(2,2)$ and $(4,3)$.
Blur and half-contrast gains hold at the tested positions, while noise and
requantization costs persist. The downscaling gain is largest at $(3,3)$,
small at $(4,3)$, and negative at $(2,2)$. We do not attribute this solely to
scalar attenuation because resizing mixes block content. Position dependence
makes same-position comparisons necessary, but not sufficient for broad fairness.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\textbf{Interpretation.} In this small evaluation DP-QIM lowers histogram
detectability relative to QIM at low payload and improves some processing
robustness measures, while losing others. It is not an undetectable watermark
and should not be recommended for covert use from these results. Whether
hybrids or gain-invariant QIM offer a better trade-off remains untested.

\textbf{Correction record.} Earlier evaluations contained frequency confounds,
test-data fitting, inappropriate small-sample KS comparisons, and unstable
payload seeds. The v2 audit additionally missed duplicate source aliases and
inconsistent outer folds. The corrected v3 run removes the alias, validates
hashes, and fits all detector components within one outer split. It corrects
both the cellwise conditioning and periodic-decoding arguments. Superseded
results remain in the repository for transparency; their numerical claims
are withdrawn. Changes in AUC cannot be assigned to deduplication alone,
because fitting and aggregation were also corrected.

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Data and uncertainty.} Only 43 crops from 14 photographs,
one fixed split and one selection seed. Conditional bootstrap intervals
do not include retraining or dataset-selection variability. Hash checks
remove exact duplicates, not semantic or near duplicates. Standard independent
benchmarks such as Kodak or DIV2K remain necessary. These photographs were also
used during method development; cross-validation is not an untouched final test.
\item \textbf{Baselines.} Only lattice QIM is compared. Gain-invariant
variants~\cite{PerezGonzalez2005rdm,Ourique2005angleqim,Li2007perceptualqim}
and learned watermarks~\cite{Zhu2018hidden,Tancik2020stegastamp} are needed.
Their relative advantages cannot be inferred from this experiment.
\item \textbf{Attacks and detectors.} Histogram jitter is not the published
UnMarker algorithm; regeneration is not evaluated. The evaluated detectors
use all-block histograms rather than exploiting the fixed public selection
seed. Rich-model or CNN steganalyzers~\cite{Fridrich2012richmodels} may do better.
One fixed noise realization per image shape is another limitation.
\item \textbf{Theory and implementation.} One bit per block at one coefficient
position; $M>1$ was numerically fragile. Finite pools, empirical ties and rounding
separate the implementation from the idealized theorem. Sampling conditionally
on original magnitude could change both distortion and distribution and would
require a new proof, not an assumption that Prop.~\ref{prop:ks} still applies.
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
Replacing lattice snapping with cellwise natural sampling changes the
detectability/robustness trade-off, but does not make a watermark invisible.
The corrected small-sample evaluation finds lower learned-histogram AUC than
QIM at low payload, increasing to 0.96 for DP-QIM at full density. Gains under
some processing operations coexist with losses under JPEG, noise and our
simplified removal stress test. The mixture theorem is idealized, and
positive-scaling invariance requires a zero boundary. Stronger baselines,
independent datasets and repeated training are needed before security claims.
